summary: This experimental RFC defines an EDNS0 extension for a validating resolver using a forwarding resolver. One query requests a complete validation path along with the answer, reducing queries and latency. It requires source-verified transport such as TCP or UDP with cookies.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking many separate questions, you ask once and get the answer plus the proof.

questions: dnssec validation path in one query
what is dns chain query option
how does chain reduce dnssec latency
subtitle: Get the full validation chain in one query instead of many.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC validation requires a client to make many separate queries to build a complete chain of trust from the root down to the target name. This multiplies latency and network traffic, especially on high-latency links.
tldr.mechanism: CHAIN is an EDNS0 extension that lets a forwarding resolver ask a recursive resolver for a complete validation chain in a single query. The resolver returns the answer plus all intermediate DNS records required for DNSSEC validation in one response.
tldr.outcome: The protocol is experimental. It reduces latency and queries for DNSSEC validation but requires both client and server support. Deployment has been limited.

today: RFC 7901 remains Experimental and has not been updated or obsoleted. CHAIN is defined as an EDNS0 extension for use between forwarding resolvers and recursive resolvers. Practical deployment of CHAIN has been limited; while the mechanism is sound, widespread adoption requires support in both clients and servers, which has not materialized.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A traditional DNS client sends a query to a recursive resolver and waits for an answer. When DNSSEC validation is enabled, the client cannot just trust that answer; it must verify the signature chain all the way from the root. This requires obtaining intermediate DNS records from multiple zones: the root, the top-level domain (TLD), the domain itself, and any subdomains in the path.

Traditionally, applications would send out many UDP queries concurrently, each waiting for an intermediate piece of the chain. This wastes bandwidth, consumes CPU and memory on the client, and causes extra latency, especially on high-latency network links. The CHAIN EDNS0 extension solves this by allowing a client to request the complete chain in a single query. The recursive resolver performs all the lookups and returns the answer plus all necessary validation records in one response.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally you have to ask the server many questions to check a DNS answer is real. CHAIN lets you ask one question and get all the answers at once.

sections.title: How CHAIN Works
sections.content:
CHAIN is an EDNS0 option that can be sent in a DNS query. It specifies the closest trust point: the lowest level of the DNS hierarchy for which the client already has a DNSSEC-validated answer in its cache. For example, if a client already validated that the com. zone is secure, it sets the closest trust point to com. and asks for www.example.com. The server does not need to return the entire chain from the root; it only sends the chain starting from just below the trust point.

In the response, the recursive resolver includes the answer to the original question in the Answer Section (as usual) and places all intermediate DNS records required for validation in the Authority Section. These records include DS records (delegation signers), DNSKEY records (zone keys), and RRSIG records (signatures).

If the client's cache is out of date or the requested chain cannot be constructed, the server may respond with an empty CHAIN option or a partial chain, allowing the client to ask again with an updated trust point.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the server the furthest point in the DNS chain you already trust. The server looks up everything from there down to your target and sends it all back in one package.

sections.title: Discovery and Support
sections.content:
A client can discover whether a server supports CHAIN by sending a zero-length CHAIN option in a regular query over any transport. If the server supports CHAIN and is willing to serve it, it responds with a zero-length CHAIN option in the answer.

CHAIN can only be used safely over source-IP-verified transports to prevent DNS amplification attacks. TCP connections are naturally verified (the three-way handshake proves the sender owns the IP address). For UDP, clients must use DNS cookies (EDNS Cookie option, defined in RFC 7873), which also verify the source IP.

Once a client learns that a server supports CHAIN, it can issue subsequent queries with CHAIN options containing the closest trust point. The client SHOULD remember which servers do not support CHAIN and fall back to traditional DNS queries for those servers.
sections.plainLanguage: First you ask if the server can do CHAIN. If it says yes, you can keep sending CHAIN requests to get the full chain faster.

sections.title: Protocol Details and Data Format
sections.content:
The CHAIN EDNS0 option has an option code of 13. It contains a single variable-length field: the closest trust point, an FQDN in DNS wire format (binary encoding, without compression).

A query with a CHAIN option MUST also have the DNSSEC OK (DO) bit set in the OPT record, indicating the client understands DNSSEC. If the DO bit is not set, or if the Checking Disabled (CD) bit is set, the server MUST ignore the CHAIN option.

In the response, the server confirms CHAIN by including the CHAIN option with the lowest trust point that was included in the returned chain. It MAY return a partial chain if the complete chain would be too large, in which case the client can retry with an updated trust point to get the remaining records.
sections.plainLanguage: The CHAIN option is a tiny piece of extra data in the DNS query that says where to start the chain. The server sends it back to say what it included.

sections.title: Practical Considerations
sections.content:
Session management: CHAIN queries are best used over TCP to get reliable delivery of large answers. Keeping the TCP connection open (using TCP keepalive, defined in RFC 7828) reduces latency for subsequent queries.

Namespace records: The CHAIN response should include the authoritative NS records for the zone and the address records (A or AAAA) for the nameservers, so a client can switch to recursive mode if needed. However, NS records from parent zones are not signed and should not be included.

Negative trust anchors: If a CHAIN answer would include data that intersects with a negative trust anchor (a zone known to be broken), the server should return a partial chain up to the negative trust anchor.

Anycast: Servers deployed using anycast should be careful with CHAIN over UDP, because different anycast nodes might not support CHAIN, and the client might see inconsistent behavior between queries.
sections.plainLanguage: CHAIN works best over TCP and long-lived connections. The server includes the nameserver addresses so the client can look them up later if needed. If a zone is known to be broken, the server stops the chain there.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Amplification attacks: A CHAIN answer can be much larger than a regular DNS answer, making it attractive as an amplification vector for spoofed-source DDoS attacks. To prevent this, servers MUST NOT return CHAIN answers over UDP unless the source IP is verified (e.g., using DNS cookies). Responses over TCP are safe because the three-way handshake proves ownership of the source IP.

Additional load: Generating CHAIN answers requires the server to do more work, looking up multiple records and building a chain. Servers are free to refuse CHAIN queries by responding with a zero-length CHAIN option if overloaded.

Privacy: A client requesting a CHAIN option reveals slightly more about its cache contents than a regular DNS client, potentially allowing fingerprinting across network reconnections. Clients concerned about privacy can use encrypted DNS transport (DNS-over-TLS or DNS-over-HTTPS) or a VPN.
sections.plainLanguage: CHAIN responses are big, so attackers could use them to flood networks. That is why servers only send CHAIN over verified connections like TCP. CHAIN also leaks a tiny bit about what the client already knows.
